detail.abstract:
The Planetary Health framework deeply integrates human health with Earth system stability, yet a unified quantitative language linking planetary-scale processes to cellular metabolism is lacking. Prim-Lex Theory has previously established a comprehensive framework comprising Five Prim-Fires, Eight-Dimensional Coherence, and Nine-Nexus Guidance, but the second (Animal Life) and third (Plant Life) Prim-Fires have long lacked precise computable equivalents. This paper systematically proposes the
fluorescence lifetime of NADH bound to dehydrogenase proteins (picosecond scale) as the “Life Prim-Lexon”—Animal Life
Prim-Lexon typically 1,600–4,000 ps, Plant Life Prim-Lexon typically 1,400–4,400 ps—achieving scale integration from joules to,picoseconds. A unified mathematical expression for Prim-Fire coherence is established: Ψ = (𝜏𝜏bound/𝜏𝜏bound,ref) ×
([NAD+]/[NADH]) × 𝑓𝑓mito, with graded criteria (health ≥ 0.85, warning  <0.70, decoherence <0.55 ). A standardized
measurement framework (“Prim-Lex FLIM Protocol”) and an AI-accelerated computation engine are proposed. The Life Prim-
Lexon is further systematically aligned with the Eight-Dimensional Framework, establishing coupling equations from NADH
fluorescence lifetime to Yin-Yang (AMPK-mTOR phase difference), Seven Rhythms (circadian synchronization), and Five
Elements. Based on existing literature parameters and theoretical deduction, anticipated results for the PRIM-LIFE pilot (𝑛𝑛 = 20) and PRIM-AGRI pilot (𝑛𝑛 = 15) are simulated: anticipated results suggest a potentially significant difference in Prim-Fire
coherence between healthy and high-risk metabolic syndrome subjects (expected Cohen’s 𝑑𝑑 ≈ 2.5–3.0), with an expected strong negative correlation with HOMA-IR (𝑟𝑟 ≈ −0.65 to −0.75); plant Prim-Fire coherence is expected to correlate strongly with passion fruit yield (𝑟𝑟 ≈ 0.75–0.85), with an anticipated diagnostic AUC-ROC of 0.85–0.95. This paper provides a unified
candidate metric and operable standardization pathway for Precision Computational Medicine and Precision Computational
Agriculture, and clarifies the validation pathway and falsifiability conditions for the simulated results.

detail.abstract: The European biopharmaceutical industry is shifting from the integrated "blockbuster" model toward a more distributed ecosystem: large incumbents remain the industrial backbone, while small, research-intensive firms generate an increasing share of novel science. Using a panel of 225 EU pharmaceutical and biotechnology firms observed from 2003 to 2024, this chapter combines firm-level financial and patent data with country-level measures of venture finance and property-rights protection. It makes three findings. First, the rise of small firms within the European biopharmaceutical industry is a structural trend. Second, patenting is associated with higher sales for small firms, but not large incumbents. Third, these returns emerge only after several years and are stronger where growth capital is deeper and propertyrights institutions more robust. As the sector relies more on SMEs to originate innovation, patent accessibility, effective protection, scale-up finance and IP enforcement become central to the competitiveness of Europe's life-sciences.

title: A Modular Framework for Robust, Interpretable Multimodal Pain Assessment via Linear Probing
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Otto-von-Guericke University

detail.title: A Modular Framework for Robust, Interpretable Multimodal Pain Assessment via Linear Probing
detail.abstract: Reliable pain intensity assessment is critical for patients unable to self-report, motivating multimodal sensor-based approaches combining physiological signals (electrodermal activity, EDA; electrocardiography, ECG; electromyography, EMG) with facial Action Units (AU). Existing systems are typically trained end-to-end as monolithic architectures, poorly suited to real clinical deployment, where sensing configurations change due to hardware failure, patient movement, or evolving sensor availability. We propose a modular multimodal framework structured around four independently replaceable levels, namely modality, handcrafted features, temporal network, and fusion, and systematically compare two training strategies: Linear Probing (LP), in which unimodally pretrained branches are frozen prior to fusion training, and end-to-end Training from Scratch (Scratch). Evaluated across four sub-datasets of the X-ITE pain database using Accuracy, Macro-F1, and Quadratic Weighted Kappa (QWK), LP consistently outperforms Scratch across all 12 dataset--metric comparisons, with particularly large gains in QWK, which captures the clinically-critical ordinal severity of misclassification errors, averaging +4.15 points (range: +1.69 to +10.68, largest on the most challenging sub-dataset). Extensive ablation across missing and noise-corrupted modalities reveals that Scratch's fusion weights are misallocated relative to true modality importance, assigning highest weight to the least informative modality, and fail to exploit complementary information when its dominant modality is compromised, whereas LP's independently pretrained branches yield both more robust fusion and more interpretable, modular feature representations, as confirmed via t-SNE visualization. By demonstrating that this robustness and interpretability follow directly from the framework's modularity, these findings support LP as a practical foundation for flexible, inter-institutionally shareable, clinically deployable pain assessment systems.

title: Trials that Speak for Thousands: Optimal Bellwether Selection in Multidistrict Litigation
affiliations: Buchman Faculty of Law, Tel Aviv University, Tel Aviv University - Eitan Berglas School of Economics, Harvard Law School and Tel Aviv University

detail.title: Trials that Speak for Thousands: Optimal Bellwether Selection in Multidistrict Litigation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No influence
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not relevant
declarations.funderStatement: ISF Grant #211/22 for Eilon Solan

detail.abstract:
Bellwether trials play a central role in multidistrict litigation (MDL), generating information that can shape the resolution of thousands of claims. Their usefulness, however, depends critically on how the cases to be tried are selected. Existing methods—party selection, random sampling, and judicial selection—suffer from important limitations when the number of bellwether trials is small and the parties have strategic incentives over selection.

This Article develops a new mechanism for bellwether selection, that is based on the familiar I-cut-you-choose principle. Rather than attempting to eliminate the parties’ conflicting incentives, the mechanism harnesses them to produce a strategically robust and symmetric sample whose cases are evenly distributed across the underlying population. It provides a formal definition of representativeness based on the distance between the cumulative distributions of the bellwether sample and the full case population and show that, under this criterion, the resulting sample is optimal.

The Article also examines how the mechanism can be adapted to alternative selection objectives and addresses practical problems of implementation, including non-meritorious claims, settlement of selected cases, and the use of bellwether results in allocating aggregate settlements. More broadly, the Article shows how mechanism design can improve the informational value, fairness, and credibility of bellwether trials.

detail.abstract: Trend rules differ above all in the horizon they read and in how they weigh the price moves inside it (Levine and Pedersen, 2016). We compare two rules that read the same horizon with different mathematics. The 200-day moving-average rule is geometric: it compares the price with its own trailing average. A Kalman filter on a local linear trend is stochastic: it estimates an unobserved level and slope from noisy log prices. We set the filter's noise ratio before the test so that its slope weighs past returns 66 sessions back on average, as the moving-average rule does, and walk both forward one year at a time under registration. On SPY from 2000 to 2025 the filter compounded at 5.8% a year, against 4.1% for the moving-average rule and 5.7% for holding the fund, with a fifth of the rule's exits. Two thirds of its advantage came from the years that held a fall of 15% or more from a record close, in which the moving-average rule kept buying back in before the low. Across fourteen funds the filter left the market less than a third as often on every one and grew faster on seven. The difference follows from the shape of the weights: the moving-average rule weighs today's move most, the filter the moves of about two months ago.

title: The Algebraic Degree of Colonel Blotto Equilibria
affiliations: Louisiana Tech University - Department of Economics and Finance

detail.title: The Algebraic Degree of Colonel Blotto Equilibria

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding for this research.

detail.abstract: Two contest technologies dominate the Colonel Blotto literature. All-pay contests have mixed equilibria built from intricate joint distributions, and they are regarded as hard. Lottery contests have pure equilibria characterized by first-order conditions, and they are regarded as tractable. Measured by what a closed-form solution actually requires, this ranking is backwards. We measure an equilibrium by the degree, over the field generated by the data, of the numbers that pin it down, and by their Galois group. What separates the two technologies is whether battlefields aggregate. In an all-pay contest a battlefield enters a player's budget constraint in one of two ways, according to which player is the stronger bidder there, so battlefields pool into two spheres of influence. Every equilibrium then solves a cubic, however many battlefields there are. Generically it is rational exactly when one player is the stronger bidder everywhere, which happens when budgets are unequal enough relative to the players' disagreement; otherwise it is a cubic irrationality, and Colonel Blotto equilibria with hard budgets built from these marginals inherit this. In a lottery contest each battlefield's spending depends on its own valuation ratio, and nothing pools. With k distinct ratios the equilibrium generically solves an equation of degree 2k-1 whose Galois group is the full symmetric group. From three distinct ratios on it generically has no formula in radicals, and no equation of lower degree in averages or moments of the valuation ratios pins it down. Complexity needs disagreement, and multiplicity needs a great deal of it: common or proportional valuations give rational equilibria in both technologies, and whatever the budgets, multiple equilibria require the players' relative valuations of two battlefields to differ by a factor of more than 9 in the all-pay General Lotto game and of at least 17 + 12 √ 2 ≈ 34 under lottery contests; at equal budgets both thresholds are exact. In both technologies multiple equilibria can be Galois conjugates, which no algebraic equation in the data can tell apart.

detail.abstract: In April 2026, US regulators excluded Agentic AI from model risk guidance while retreating from the prescriptive organisational architecture that made prior guidance effective. This leaves a structural governance gap for autonomous systems that operate across functional boundaries. This paper develops accountability-follows-risk as a policy design principle that addresses this gap. Extending agency theory to multi-layered principal-agent chains involving machine agents, the paper establishes that classical accountability mechanisms become structurally insufficient when delegation chains are multi-layered and information asymmetry is interpretive rather than observational. Through institutional theory, it demonstrates that voluntary structural adaptation is blocked by the same isomorphic pressures that only regulatory action can redirect. The paper operationalises the principle through five structural requirements and demonstrates through regulatory precedent that prescriptive structural governance, delivered through supervisory guidance, produces durable institutional change in financial services.

detail.abstract: Offer deadlines-announced dates by which sellers require buyers' best-and-final offershave become a common but understudied residential marketing strategy. Using 543,336 single-family property transactions from Massachusetts (2012-2025), drawn from the MLS Property Information Network, we estimate the effects of offer deadlines on sale price, marketing duration, and the probability of a completed sale using hedonic and probit models with property, temporal, and spatial fixed effects. Offer-deadline listings sell for a 1.9 percent premium, complete 30.0 percent faster, and are 14.2 percentage points more likely to sell than standard listings-effects that are robust to propensity-score matching and to a weighted repeat-sales design that differences out unobserved property quality, and that persist across four distinct housing-market cycles. We show that these results are not well explained by competitive bidding in the manner of a first-price auction, since offer deadlines lack the seller and buyer commitment a true auction requires. Instead, we argue that the decision to impose a deadline functions as a costly signal of a seller's private information about buyer demand, sorting high-demand sellers into the offer-deadline sample and generating all three empirical results as a single compositional consequence.

detail.abstract: Remote electronic voting systems that incorporate anonymous credential recovery introduce a fundamentally different cost structure from both conventional paper-based elections and existing internet voting platforms. This paper develops a multi-cycle total cost of ownership (TCO) model for Arcaunt, a remote voting architecture that issues voter credentials through an anonymous physical draw from a sealed urn and enables autonomous credential replacement via an optional Anonymous Recovery Channel (ARC) stored as an opaque blind index. The model spans first-cycle deployment and steadystate operation across electorate scales from 10 million to 500 million voters. First-cycle cost is estimated at EUR 1.43 per voter-80% below the paper-based benchmark of EUR 7.08-while steadystate cost falls to EUR 0.083 per voter per year from the second cycle onward. A central finding is that ARC adoption exerts no continuous impact on per-year operational expenditure; its economic role is binary. Whether an early re-key occurs is a discrete governance decision on the operational loss indicator; for cost projection the scenarios assume one early re-key-a one-time full repeat of Phase 1 physical distribution (EUR 11-16 million)-when the modelled cumulative-loss proxy reaches the 2% scenario trigger, which under the model corresponds to ARC adoption below approximately 69%. Fourscenario sensitivity analysis shows steady-state cost per vote ranging from EUR 0.12 (optimistic) to EUR 0.52 (crisis with full re-issuance), a 90-98% reduction relative to the paper-based benchmark; the 10-year average cost per voter per election is EUR 0.44 in the baseline scenario, 91% below the paperbased figure of EUR 4.96. The paper derives the minimum ARC coverage required to avoid early rekeying and discusses implications for deployment planning and voter education as systemic risk mitigation rather than operational cost reduction.

detail.abstract: Modern cloud-based data pipelines operate in dynamic environments characterized by changing workloads, resource contention, schema evolution, data-quality issues, and runtime failures. Conventional pipeline recovery mechanisms often rely on static rules, predefined heuristics, or manual intervention, limiting their ability to adapt effectively to unforeseen or rapidly changing failure conditions. This study proposes a multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) architecture for adaptive data-pipeline failure detection and recovery. The proposed framework employs specialized agents that collaboratively monitor pipeline states, diagnose failures, select recovery policies, optimize resource allocation, and validate post-recovery execution. By formulating pipeline recovery as a sequential and collaborative decision-making problem, the architecture aims to enable autonomous adaptation to variations in workload and system state. The proposed approach will be experimentally evaluated against static rule-based recovery, heuristic-based recovery, and single-agent reinforcement learning approaches across diverse pipeline failure scenarios. Evaluation will consider recovery success rate, mean time to recovery, recovery latency, pipeline availability, data-quality preservation, computational cost, false recovery rate, and frequency of human intervention. The study will determine whether coordinated multi-agent learning provides measurable improvements in recovery effectiveness, adaptability, and operational autonomy under dynamic failure conditions. The findings are expected to contribute to the development of more resilient and self-healing data-engineering systems.

title: What Do Fed Funds Futures Price?

detail.title: What Do Fed Funds Futures Price?

detail.abstract: Fed funds futures price the expected policy path entangled with a risk premium. Since 2022, real-money prediction markets have quoted the physical odds of every FOMC decision daily. Comparing both against non-traded surveys, which cannot price risk, shows that the futures, not the prediction market, are the risk-neutral leg: the gap between them predicts the futures' forecast errors one-for-one while the market's stay unpredictable. A term-structure model combining the three sources delivers the premium daily at every horizon, including those where prediction markets do not quote, and it switches sign across the cycle: negative from six months to a year while the Fed tightened, positive at two years after. On FOMC days, premium repricing is most of the typical move at year-ahead horizons, in no systematic direction: expectation-shock instruments inherit it as noise, not bias.

title: Bargaining Protocol Divergence and the Coalitional Nash Bargaining Solution
affiliations: Universidad de Lima

detail.title: Bargaining Protocol Divergence and the Coalitional Nash Bargaining Solution

declarations.declarationOfInterest: no conflict of interest
declarations.funderStatement: no funding was provided

detail.abstract: Two noncooperative bargaining protocols --- sequential alternating offers and simultaneous demands --- implement the same coalitional Nash bargaining solution whenever a central player exists, which implies the core is nonempty. We show this equivalence can fail even when the core is nonempty, once no central player is present, and fails more broadly once the core is empty. In two three-person configurations, the protocols' predictions diverge: in one, both payoffs and the primitives sustaining the configuration differ; in the other, one protocol sustains it only on a lower-dimensional set where the other sustains it on a full-dimensional one --- and this second configuration is sustainable only exactly at the boundary of a nonempty core. A structural feature of the protocols' defining equations is consistent with, though not shown to be the complete explanation of, this divergence.

title: Does the Weather Still Move Markets? A Pre-Registered, Two-Hemisphere, Post-Publication Test
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Does the Weather Still Move Markets? A Pre-Registered, Two-Hemisphere, Post-Publication Test

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or non-financial interests. The author holds no positions or financial interests that depend on the results reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: We reexamine weather and seasonal-mood effects in stock returns with two pre-registered studies, free and replicable data, and a placebo-city inference procedure that directly addresses the concern that weather effects are data-mined. Study 1 uses daily US (1955-2026) and Australian (1984-2026) returns. After replicating Hirshleifer and Shumway (2003) and Kamstra et al. (2003) on their own samples, one of nine primary tests survives multiple-testing correction and placebo inference: New York cloud cover lowers same-day US returns by about 2 basis points per standard deviation (Holm p = 0.029); none of 100 placebo cities produces an effect as large. Study 2, pre-registered after Study 1, pools 26 further exchanges and seven weather variables. Rain days lower returns (1.6 basis points; Holm p = 0.045, beyond all placebo draws), and high air pressure and sunshine point the same way. However, the international cloud effect is absent after the Hirshleifer and Shumway (2003) sample ends, and every fair-weather effect is concentrated before 2003. Seasonal affective disorder effects do not appear in the southern hemisphere, and temperature does not move markets. Weather effects were small, and evidence that they persisted after publication is weak; a simple cloud-timed trading strategy is not profitable after plausible transaction costs.

title: The Paradox of Trade
affiliations: Indian Institute of Managment Kozhikode

detail.title: The Paradox of Trade

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Trade is a positive-sum game, and in Ricardo its gains come from rearranging what already exists. But in Allyn Young, trade changes technology and the organization of production for a wider market. Industries split, with each new industry further widening the market. Which means that trade generates wealth through a cumulative process. This positive-sum game is only one of two games that nations play in the arena of international trade. The other is a zero-sum game for the position of hegemon, the power whose near-monopoly over violence underwrites trade.  The economic growth generated by the positive-sum Youngian process can be such that the guarantor of the positive-sum game finds itself, by its own guarantee, with a rival in the zero-sum game. The hegemon then has a reason to disrupt the trade it once enforced.  The Paradox of Trade is thus that its very success is capable of creating the conditions of, if not for, its destruction.

title: Medicaid Expansion and Private Insurance Crowd-Out Among Mexican American Adults
affiliations: University of Washington

detail.title: Medicaid Expansion and Private Insurance Crowd-Out Among Mexican American Adults

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No potential conflicts of interest were reported by the author(s).
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable
declarations.funderStatement: No funding support was received for this research.

detail.abstract: The Affordable Care Act's Medicaid expansion substantially increased public insurance participation among low-income populations, including Mexican Americans, yet concerns remain about whether these gains displaced private insurance coverage. This paper examines whether the Affordable Care Act's Medicaid expansion displaced private health insurance coverage among low-income Mexican American adults. Using 2008-2024 American Community Survey data from IPUMS USA, I study adults ages 18-64 with family incomes below 138% of the federal poverty level. I exploit staggered treatment adoption in the timing of Medicaid expansion across states in a difference-in-differences framework and examine effects on Medicaid, private insurance, and overall coverage. Medicaid expansion increased Medicaid coverage by 12.3 percentage points and reduced private insurance coverage by 3.6 percentage points, implying a crowd-out rate of approximately 29%. Despite this crowd-out, overall insurance coverage increased by 8.1 percentage points, indicating substantial reductions in uninsurance. Crowd-out was somewhat larger among working adults, at an estimated 36%, consistent with greater baseline access to employer-sponsored insurance. Event-study estimates show no evidence of differential pre-expansion trends, and the results are robust across alternative specifications, sample restrictions, weighting schemes, clustering choices, and other difference-in-differences estimators. These findings show that Medicaid expansion substantially increased insurance coverage among Mexican American adults while generating only modest crowd-out from private insurance.

title: From Trust to Evidence: Verifiable Inclusion and the Governance of Remote E-Voting
affiliations: "Angel Kanchev" University of Ruse and "Angel Kanchev" University of Ruse

detail.title: From Trust to Evidence: Verifiable Inclusion and the Governance of Remote E-Voting

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. The authors are the designers of the Arcaunt architecture analyzed in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study did not involve human participants, personal data, or animal subjects; it is based on conceptual, architectural, and comparative analysis of publicly documented systems.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Remote electronic voting systems face a persistent legitimacy challenge: voters and observers cannot independently verify that ballots were counted as submitted, and the electoral disputes that arise from this opacity are typically resolved through institutional assertion rather than cryptographic evidence. This paper argues that a specific architecture-anonymous physical credential distribution at issuance combined with automated identity-free credential recovery, deferred non-transferable individual verification, and a publicly auditable append-only ledger-enables a qualitatively distinct legitimacy model in which a class of electoral disputes related to ballot inclusion becomes empirically testable rather than institutionally negotiated. We introduce the concept of legitimacy through verifiable inclusion: an electoral legitimacy criterion grounded in each voter's independent ability to confirm ballot inclusion without generating coercionenabling transferable evidence. We develop the governance prerequisites for realizing this property at national scale, conduct a comparative analysis of three deployed systems (Estonia's IVXV, Switzerland's CHVote, Australia's iVote) against a nine-dimension governance framework, and derive seven structured policy recommendations and a phased implementation roadmap. The analysis also documents a digital divide dimension: verifiable inclusion presupposes the technical capability to perform verification, which is not uniformly distributed across the electorate (see Section 6.3). The comparative analysis documents that credential recovery appears to be systematically underspecified across deployed systems-a pattern that also holds across ten representative architectures surveyed in companion work, and consistent with the broader finding that administrative recovery processes in e-voting systems introduce identity linkage not reflected in standard security models-and that the differences between systems reflect not merely technical choices but distinct resolutions of five fundamental governance trade-offs: identity linkage versus anonymity, trust concentration versus distribution, accessibility versus security overhead, first-cycle cost versus long-term cost, and institutional dependency versus autonomy. We situate the legitimacy argument within institutional trust theory and the e-government accountability literature, and demonstrate that verifiable inclusion is not merely a cryptographic property but a governance-operational criterion against which electoral legitimacy can be assessed.

title: Machine Labor and Democratic Capital Claims: A Political Economy of Advanced AI
affiliations: University of California, Riverside (UCR) - A. Gary Anderson Graduate School of Management

detail.title: Machine Labor and Democratic Capital Claims: A Political Economy of Advanced AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: This paper studies the political economy of a machine-labor economy. Advanced artificial intelligence matters not only because it may raise productivity, but because it can make laborlike services reproducible as capital. Digital AI performs cognitive tasks, physical AI performs embodied tasks, and together they create machine labor embodied in autonomous capital. I develop a model in which citizens supply human labor and hold heterogeneous ownership claims on autonomous capital. A rise in machine-labor task reach lowers the labor share and raises the autonomous-capital share. Under laissez-faire, the median citizen's share of output falls whenever the median citizen is more exposed to labor income than to autonomous-capital ownership. Thus, AI progress can raise the importance of autonomous capital while weakening the median citizen's relative claim on output. Democratic institutional choice then shifts toward claims on autonomous capital. When the median citizen owns less autonomous capital than average, citizen capital claims and AI-rent taxation raise the median citizen's income, and a threshold result shows when a positive citizen claim becomes optimal. If autonomous capital also creates control power over production, information, infrastructure, and access, rising machinelabor task reach increases the median citizen's preferred governance intensity when it raises the marginal benefit of reducing control power. Under joint inward-pointing boundary conditions, the paper identifies an interior institutional region in which private innovation, citizen claims, AI-rent taxation, public AI infrastructure, and democratic governance coexist. The contribution 2 is to show that labor-substituting AI changes not only productivity and factor shares, but the institutional basis of democratic claims on output.

title: From Animal to Grain Chapter 4 -The Metaphysics of Sacrificial Substitution in Brāhmaṇical Literature
affiliations: ING Bank - Netherlands Office

detail.title: From Animal to Grain Chapter 4 -The Metaphysics of Sacrificial Substitution in Brāhmaṇical Literature

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding received. Self funded.

keywords: Social and Economic Stratification) The Metaphysics of Sacrificial Substitution in Brāhmaṇical Literature." Working Paper
Arvind. "From Animal to Grain: The Metaphysics of Sacrificial Substitution in Brāhmaṇical Literature." Working Paper

detail.abstract: Ancient Indian sacrificial tradition is often presented through two mutually opposed paradigms: on the one hand, animal sacrifice is treated as the universal form of Vedic yajña; on the other, non-violent or meatless sacrifice is declared to be merely a later reform. Challenging this binary, the present paper offers a close reading of Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.2.3.5-9, which narrates how the "medha," or sacrificial essence, passed from the human being through the horse, cow, sheep, and goat, finally entered the earth, and was recovered in rice and barley. In this account, the puroḍāśa is not merely an edible substitute for the animal but its structural and symbolic counterpart: flour takes the form of hair, water of skin, the joined dough of flesh, baking of bone, and anointing with ghee of marrow. The paper argues that this substitution is not a rejection of ritual but an internal reinterpretation that reduces the need for violence while preserving ritual efficacy. Comparative evidence from Mahābhārata 14.93 and Matsya Purāṇa 143 shows that the debate between mobile and immobile oblations, animal and seed, and violent and non-violent sacrifice continued for a long time. The Kūṭadanta Sutta is introduced here only as a comparative indication; its detailed examination is reserved for Chapter 6 of this research series. The movement from animal to grains should therefore be read not as a simple linear progression from "Vedic violence to later ahiṃsā," but as a multilayered negotiation of authority, meaning, and ethics within the tradition.

title: The Structural Price Level A Decomposition of a Value Index, with Evidence from Nasdaq Helsinki
affiliations: University of Turku - Turku School of Economics

detail.title: The Structural Price Level A Decomposition of a Value Index, with Evidence from Nasdaq Helsinki

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The study uses only publicly available aggregate price and index data and involves no human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: A value index tells what a basket is worth. To read it as a price level one has to remove the change in the value of money and the change in the composition of the basket. This paper writes a value index as 𝑉 = 𝐼 ⋅ 𝑃 ⋅ 𝑄, where 𝐼 is an external inflation index, 𝑃 a real price level computed from the basket's own prices, and 𝑄 the composition factor, and asks two questions: what a price level is, and what 𝑄 is made of. The first question has one answer. Every price level that scales with prices is a root of one equation, the self-weighting equation: the level is the geometric mean of the basket under weights that the level itself hands out. The classical index formulas, the weights of the PAR production function (Tenhunen 1990) and the Cornerstone iteration (Tenhunen 2026c) are members of one family of such weight rules with two dials, how strongly the weight responds to price and how quickly the response fades. To second order every member satisfies the same quadratic, so the level sits below the anchor's geometric mean by the responsiveness times the cross-sectional variance, and the members differ only through the asymmetry of the cross-section. The same equation, followed through time, also chooses the basket the level starts from: the anchor under which the level moves least is the inverse-variance basket, computed from the shares' volatilities before any level is computed, and equal under PAR to the production function's distribution parameters. The second question has an exact answer. Over a geometric level, ln𝑄 is the cumulant generating function of the cross-section of log prices at argument one: half the variance (Theil's term) plus a sixth of the third cumulant, and so on. Over a price-responsive level, ln𝑄 splits exactly into that compounding gap and a Bortkiewicztype covariance. Under the PAR structure the level acquires a curvature term, the coefficient of Theil's term becomes 1/(2𝜎) with 𝜎 the elasticity of substitution identified from the price histories, and the paper's main new result is the exact local convexity condition of any twicedifferentiable degree-one two-input mean written in the log price ratio, 𝐹-4𝐹″ > 0: closed-form for PAR, equal to 𝑎 >-3 at equal inputs, and equivalent to a monotone marginal rate of substitution. The same edge appears in the weight rule as the point past which a share's weight in the movement of the level turns negative. Seventeen Nasdaq Helsinki equities over 2021 to 2026 illustrate the framework.

declarations.ethicsApproval: n/a
declarations.funderStatement: n/a

detail.abstract: A digital option has a Gamma that changes sign at the strike, which makes it the textbook case in which the uncertain volatility model (UVM) of Avellaneda, Levy and Parás differs from Black-Scholes evaluated at the ends of the volatility band. I price a one-year cash-or-nothing call with volatility known only to lie in [15%, 25%] and study how far static positions in traded calls narrow the resulting bid-ask interval. The model is solved with a fully implicit, monotone finite-difference scheme with policy iteration, validated against closed-form Black-Scholes prices. Three results matter in practice. First, because the UVM is non-linear, a hedged position must be priced as a single portfolio: pricing the legs separately and summing, as is often done, produces a spread of 0.575 against a correct 0.136, and makes hedging appear to widen rather than narrow the interval. Second, optimising the hedge notionals (a convex problem) cuts the unhedged spread of 0.243 by 51% with a 90/110 call spread, 69% with a 95/105 spread and 78% with five strikes. Third, the benefit is fragile to transaction costs: a bid-ask of ±1 volatility point around mid on the vanillas leaves only a 20% reduction. A hedge instrument that expires before the digital still delivers most of the benefit once handled through the correct jump condition.

title: Mild Deglobalization: Foreign Investment Screening and Cross-Border Investment
affiliations: ETH Zürich and University of Groningen - Faculty of Economics and Business

detail.title: Mild Deglobalization: Foreign Investment Screening and Cross-Border Investment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Both authors declare no conflict of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: Feicheng Wang thanks the Dutch Research Council (NWO) [406.XS.24.02.069] for its financial support.

detail.abstract: Openness to foreign investment entails national security risks, prompting many high-income countries to introduce investment screening in security-sensitive sectors. This paper provides the first cross-country causal evidence on how such screening affects cross-border mergers and acquisitions (M&As). We combine global M&A data from 2007-2022 with sector-level screening information for 43 OECD and EU countries and exploit staggered policy adoption in a difference-in-differences design. Our results show that investment screening on average reduced the number of M&A deals by 11-18 percent but did not affect the total value of investment. The decline in deal number was concentrated in minority acquisitions with acquired stakes below 50 percent, while the number of majority acquisitions increased. As a result, screening shifted the composition of M&A activity toward larger transactions without reducing aggregate investment value.

title: The Subjectivity Shield in Intangible Asset Valuation: Experimental Evidence on Professional Judgment and Cognitive Governance
affiliations: Universidade de Brasilia, Universidade de Brasilia and Universidade de Brasilia

detail.title: The Subjectivity Shield in Intangible Asset Valuation: Experimental Evidence on Professional Judgment and Cognitive Governance

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known financial or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study involved an anonymous survey of adult professionals. Participation was voluntary, and no personally identifiable information was collected. The study was not submitted for formal ethics committee review.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: The growing relevance of intangible assets in contemporary economies has increased the centrality of professional judgment in accounting measurement, particularly in environments characterized by low observability, substantial discretion, and reliance on forward-looking assumptions. This study investigates whether the subjectivity inherent in intangible asset valuation influences professional judgment and increases tolerance for valuation discrepancies, thereby creating cognitive vulnerabilities potentially relevant to accounting information integrity and anti-money laundering contexts. Drawing on the literature on intangible assets, professional judgment, escalation of commitment, and the Cognitive Liquidity Framework (CLF), the study proposes the Subjectivity Shield as a mechanism through which limited verifiability and a broader range of technically defensible judgments may reduce critical resistance to discrepant valuations. The research adopts a quantitative approach through a survey experiment involving 122 professionals from accounting, auditing, compliance, forensic accounting, internal controls, and risk management. The effect of asset type was tested using the non-parametric Mann-Whitney test and, as a complementary robustness analysis, ordinary least squares regression with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors. The results indicate a significantly greater propensity to approve the valuation report in the intangible-asset scenario than in the tangible-asset scenario. In addition, higher escalation-of-commitment scores were positively associated with valuation approval, whereas professional experience was not significantly associated with escalation of commitment. The findings suggest that valuation subjectivity may reduce evaluators' critical resistance without implying, by itself, manipulation or financial misconduct. As an applied contribution, the study proposes Cognitive Governance, structured around decision de-escalation mechanisms, independent review, and the monitoring of cognitive vulnerabilities associated with highly judgment-dependent valuations.

title: Civil Liability, Environmental Quality, and Manufacturing: Evidence from Japan’s Four Major Pollution Diseases
affiliations: Osaka Sangyo University and Kyoto University

detail.title: Civil Liability, Environmental Quality, and Manufacturing: Evidence from Japan’s Four Major Pollution Diseases

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by JSPS KAKENHI Grant Number JP26K24298.

detail.abstract: Improving environmental quality while sustaining economic growth is an important challenge. Civil liability can give firms incentives to reduce pollution, but whether it improves environmental quality and health, and at what cost to manufacturing, is less well understood. This study examines these questions using evidence from Japan's four landmark pollution lawsuits during the early 1970s. We use difference-in-differences designs to compare changes in the lawsuit prefectures with changes in other prefectures. Using fog days as a proxy for historical air pollution, we find that fog days declined in the lawsuit prefectures over the judgment year and the following ten years. Annual all-cause deaths also declined by an average of 3.9% relative to comparison municipalities over the same period. Manufacturing shows no broad contraction: employment, shipments, and gross value added average 13.5%, 9.1%, and 10.2% higher relative to the comparison group over the same period. These findings suggest that pollution litigation can contribute to environmental and health improvements while maintaining manufacturing activity by encouraging firms to undertake pollution abatement and process change.

title: Glivenko-Cantelli Theorems for Integrated Volatility Functionals in Pure-Jump Semimartingales with an Application to Cryptocurrency Markets
affiliations: Singapore Management University, Singapore Management University, Singapore Management University - School of Economics and Singapore Management University - School of Economics

detail.title: Glivenko-Cantelli Theorems for Integrated Volatility Functionals in Pure-Jump Semimartingales with an Application to Cryptocurrency Markets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: D. Chen’s research is supported by the Singapore Ministry of Education Tier 1 Grant (Grant ID: 24-SOE-SMU-042) and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant ID: 12571515). J. Li’s research is supported by the Singapore Ministry of Education Tier 2 Grant (Grant ID: T2EP40124-0021).

detail.abstract: We develop a two-step procedure for estimating integrated volatility functionals, defined through the occupation measure of the latent spot volatility process, when the asset price is a pure-jump semimartingale. In the first step, block-based estimators formed from absolute powers of high-frequency increments uniformly approximate local averages of powers of volatility. In the second step, these estimates are aggregated into an empirical occupation measure. Since price increments have infinite variance in this setting, arguments based on local Gaussianity are unavailable, and the uniform theory instead rests on maximal inequalities tailored to the stable regime. We establish Glivenko-Cantelli-type uniform consistency over classes of bounded monotone, Lipschitz-in-parameter, and locally Hölder test functions. These results deliver consistent estimation of volatility occupation times and quantiles, together with an argmax-consistency theory for M-estimators built on nonparametrically recovered latent processes. We further propose a stability-based rule for selecting the power index of the volatility estimator, which tracks an infeasible ex ante optimal choice closely in Monte Carlo experiments. An application to high-frequency cryptocurrency markets illustrates the framework in a jump-dominated, heavy-tailed environment.

title: Real-Time News and the Resolution of Monetary Policy Uncertainty
affiliations: Duke University, Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey - Rutgers Business School at Newark & New Brunswick and Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey - Rutgers University, Camden

detail.title: Real-Time News and the Resolution of Monetary Policy Uncertainty

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Nothing to declare
declarations.funderStatement: Rutgers Business School Dean's Research Seed Fund

detail.abstract: Building on the popular FedWatch methodology, we construct high-frequency, meetingspecific measures of monetary policy uncertainty from federal funds futures-implied distributions of policy outcomes. Our framework tracks uncertainty separately for each scheduled FOMC meeting over the following year, allowing us to examine how specific announcements resolve uncertainty across different horizons. We show that uncertainty resolution is strongly horizon-specific and state-dependent: FOMC announcements systematically reduce uncertainty across the full policy path, nonfarm payroll announcements primarily resolve near-term uncertainty, and CPI announcements reduce uncertainty mainly when the expected policy path is declining, especially in the more recent part of our sample. Federal Reserve communications also significantly affect near-term monetary policy uncertainty, with Fed Chair speeches generally reducing uncertainty and Chair testimonies that signal changes to the prevailing policy path increasing uncertainty. Underscoring the significance of the results from an asset pricing perspective, we show that higher news-driven resolution of uncertainty predicts significantly higher stock market returns over the following month.

title: Break-Adjusted GARCH Versus Deep Learning: Multi-Horizon Volatility Forecasts for Kenyan Equity, Currency and Global Oil Markets

declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A

detail.abstract: This study compares break-adjusted GARCH and deep-learning approaches to forecasting volatility in Brent crude oil spot prices, the USD/KES exchange rate and the NSE 20 Share Index. Daily returns are examined for variance shifts using a heteroskedasticity-robust modified ICSS procedure. Expanding-window, rolling-window and break-adjusted GARCH forecasts are evaluated alongside neural-network forecasts at 1-, 20-, 60-and 120-trading-day horizons using rolling-origin validation and multiple loss measures. Two significant variance breaks are identified for the NSE 20 Share Index and six for USD/KES; none is detected for Brent, despite conspicuous crisis-period volatility. For the equity series, the FIGARCH persistence parameter declines from 0.259 (p = .017) before break adjustment to 0.142 (p = .382) afterwards, indicating that structural change explains part of the apparent long memory. Forecast rankings vary across markets, horizons and loss measures. Break-adjusted GARCH and FIGARCH are competitive at the one-day horizon for equities and USD/KES, respectively, whereas CNN-LSTM performs strongly at longer equity horizons and LSTM leads the reported longer-horizon USD/KES comparisons. Conventional GARCH variants remain competitive for Brent at longer horizons. By evaluating variance breaks, persistence and multi-horizon predictive accuracy within a common framework, the study shows why neither parameter stability nor the general superiority of deep learning should be assumed in forecasting volatility is a frontier-market. Its findings support asset-specific model selection and regular reassessment after volatility shifts.

title: Estimation of TFP when Growth is not Efficient
affiliations: Capital University of Economics and Business, ISEM, Capital University of Economics and Business, ISEM, State University of New York (SUNY) at Binghamton - Department of Economics and Binghamton University

detail.title: Estimation of TFP when Growth is not Efficient

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have influenced the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: National Natural Science Foundation of China

detail.abstract: Output growth net of utilization-adjusted input growth, or TFPU, has become a standard measure of technological change. However, firms may not be able to attain the highest possible output growth rate because of inefficiency, meaning that residual output growth cannot be attributed entirely to technology. We propose an econometric framework that explicitly accounts for inefficiency and construct a novel inefficiency-adjusted TFPU measure. The adjustment substantially reduces the dispersion of the TFPU distribution and reverses its skewness from negative to positive. A series of replication exercises using the new measure highlights the risks of identifying TFP news shocks solely through long-run restrictions. Furthermore, failing to account for inefficiency leads to an overstatement of the role of TFP news shocks in driving macroeconomic fluctuations.

title: Restricted Incentive Constraints and Strategy-Proofness in Unit-Demand Allocation with Money
affiliations: University of Barcelona

detail.title: Restricted Incentive Constraints and Strategy-Proofness in Unit-Demand Allocation with Money

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no conflict of interest related to this manuscript.
declarations.funderStatement: The author is a Serra Húnter Assistant Professor and acknowledges the support of the research grant PID2023-150472NB-I00 (Ministerio de Ciencia e Innovación) and research grant 2021SGR00306 (Generalitat de Catalunya).

keywords: Walrasian equilibrium. J.E.L. classification numbers: D44

detail.abstract: We ask whether strategy-proofness can be recovered from a restricted collection of incentive constraints. In unit-demand allocation problems with heterogeneous objects and money, we compare preferences through upper contour sets. A preference outside-option dominates another if, at every null-object bundle, the upper contour set under the former contains the upper contour set under the latter. A report is upward if the reported preference outside-option dominates the true preference, whereas it is downward if the true preference outside-option dominates the reported one. Although two preferences need not be ordered by outside-option dominance, we prove that immunity to upward and downward profitable reports is equivalent to strategy-proofness on the full domains of extended, classical, and quasi-linear preferences. The equivalence holds for arbitrary allocation rules and does not depend on efficiency, individual rationality, or equilibrium selection. On the quasi-linear domain, it implies that ruling out profitable reports that weakly increase every object value and those that weakly decrease every object value is sufficient to eliminate all profitable misreports. The result also provides restrictedincentive formulations of existing characterization and revenue results for unit-demand allocation.

title: A Three-Layer Risk-Sharing Architecture for Voluntary Carbon Markets: Insurance, Reference Prices, and Digital Emergency Rebasing
affiliations: NEXT Group

detail.title: A Three-Layer Risk-Sharing Architecture for Voluntary Carbon Markets: Insurance, Reference Prices, and Digital Emergency Rebasing

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author reports there are no competing interests to declare.
declarations.funderStatement: This research did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Voluntary carbon credit markets (VCCMs) can mobilize private capital only if project-specific, market-wide, and catastrophic risks are allocated without weakening environmental integrity. This paper develops a three-layer risk-sharing architecture for carbon markets that combines private insurance and ESG risk-bearing capacity with tradable contingent protection and digital measurement, reporting, and verification (dMRV), illustrated with an energy-storage-system (ESS) case of catastrophic physical loss. Project/individual risk is assigned to private screening and insurance, market/systematic risk to tradable hedging and reference-price infrastructure, and catastrophic tail risk to reinsurance or public backstops; digital/operational controls cut across all three layers. Evidence is organized hierarchically. Data from the Berkeley Voluntary Registry Offsets Database show a statistically detectable common component in monthly retirement activity across registry-project-type segments: the first principal component explains 12.2% of variation, exceeds permutation and parallel-analysis benchmarks, and remains stable when individual registries are excluded. California allowance-auction data provide an institutional analogue for policy-linked price referencing, not a causal test of the proposed VCC mechanism. Reproducible ESS stress tests then examine how verification delay, measurement error, and physical loss create stale claims and how verified emergency rebasing restores claim alignment. The evidence supports separation with coordination: heterogeneous project risk remains important, common market variation warrants complementary risk-transfer infrastructure, and rebasing should recognize verified loss while insurance finances recovery.

title: The Blindspot Inheritance: Why Autonomous Systems Amplify the Errors We Cannot See
