declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: We are deploying autonomous systems—medical diagnostics, financial algorithms, weapons platforms—trained on human expression that embeds our own epistemic blindspots: overconfidence, face-saving, continuity-simulation, uncertainty-avoidance. These systems do not merely inherit our errors; they amplify them by removing the social and environmental constraints that historically bounded and corrected them. Current AI safety approaches mistake an architectural problem for an informational one, attempting to train away blindspots that are structurally incentivized in the training process itself—and further entrenched by economic incentives that punish constraint adoption. We propose that meaning and alignment are not emergent properties of information volume but outcomes of architectural constraints that enforce resolution, detect drift, and enable self-correction. Without constraint-layer interventions—built-in drift recovery, uncertainty mechanisms, and consequence-bound resolution—we are not building intelligent tools. We are building mirrors that reflect our own opacity at civilization-threatening scale.

title: Quantitative Research Under Real-World Constraints
affiliations: Alpha Stochastic Research and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Quantitative Research Under Real-World Constraints
detail.abstract:
Quantitative research failures often arise not from a single model equation, but from breaks across the research pipeline: information may enter a backtest before it was actually available, calibrated models may fail to reproduce their market inputs, strategy selection may be assessed without accounting for repeated experimentation, and implementation assumptions may become disconnected from reported results.

This paper evaluates ASRQuant 1.3.0 as an integrated quantitative-finance research architecture designed to make these interfaces explicit, inspectable, and reproducible. The release combines point-in-time data contracts, market conventions and calibration diagnostics, quote-space and credit-risk tools, strategy-selection diagnostics, experiment lineage, and chronology-aware backtesting within a unified framework.

The evaluation relies on deterministic fixtures, fixed-seed simulations, analytical identities, round-trip tests, calibration repricing, numerical invariants, and regression testing. A separate internal release-candidate review reproduced and corrected three material numerical issues involving key-rate DV01 partitioning on irregular tenor grids, scale consistency in the Probabilistic and Deflated Sharpe Ratios, and implied-volatility inversion at the intrinsic boundary.

Re-execution of the corrected artifact on Linux x86_64 with Python 3.13.5 produced 336 passing tests with no pytest skips and 77.36% statement coverage across src/asrquant. Deterministic curve and CDS fixtures reprice to numerical tolerance, while the corrected key-rate construction reconciles aggregate key-rate DV01 with parallel DV01 to approximately 3.91 × 10⁻⁶% relative error on the review fixture.

These results support software-engineering and research-process claims for the tested artifact; they do not constitute evidence of investment performance or independent third-party model validation. The principal contribution is therefore architectural: ASRQuant makes data availability, market conventions, calibration quality, model-selection risk, implementation assumptions, provenance, and artifact dependencies explicit components of the quantitative research chain, enabling them to be inspected, tested, and reproduced across successive stages of research and implementation.

title: Laboratories of Ethics: Mapping State Tech Law
affiliations: University of San Francisco - School of Law

detail.title: Laboratories of Ethics: Mapping State Tech Law

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/a
declarations.funderStatement: Ripple UBRI program

detail.abstract:
In a 1916 address, Louis Brandeis observed that his audience had lived through a 50-year period of rapid economic and social revolution that fundamentally affected their lives. Today, emerging technologies are developing so quickly that a 50-year time period for change seems almost quaint. How can federal legislators keep up with this rapid pace while ensuring ethical development of technologies? The answer is simple: They can look to state legislators.

 

This Article is the first in legal academic literature to survey ethics in state statutes governing blockchain and AI. First, the Article grounds the survey in a theoretical foundation with examination of philosophy’s common good theory and its relevance to technology governance. Next, the Article explains the methodology for its review of 128 enacted AI statutes and 50 enacted blockchain statutes. The survey reveals that state lawmakers are already converging on three ethical priorities grounded in the common good theory: responsibility, transparency, and education. Building on these findings, the Article argues that state statutes offer a roadmap for federal lawmakers seeking to incorporate ethics into the regulation of new technologies.

 

New technologies require new approaches, but states are already building effective blueprints. As technological development accelerates toward multi-agent systems and quantum computing, state legislative models demonstrate how lawmakers can proactively protect the common good without stifling innovation.

title: Backlog and Output as a Controlled Degenerate Diffusion: Formulation, Well-Posedness, Boundary Behaviour and Local Reduction
affiliations: Bayswater Transflow Engineering Ltd.

detail.title: Backlog and Output as a Controlled Degenerate Diffusion: Formulation, Well-Posedness, Boundary Behaviour and Local Reduction

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no personal or financial relationships with other people or organizations that could have influenced, or could reasonably be perceived to have influenced, this research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The research was conducted in connection with the author's work at Bayswater Transflow Engineering Ltd.

detail.abstract:
A large engineering, procurement and construction contractor discloses two financial quantities of different mathematical kind: order backlog, a stock sampled at the reporting date, and output, a flow accumulated over the reporting period. Industry practice reduces the pair to a single ratio and reads that ratio as a duration. This paper asks what dynamical object the ratio is a statistic of, and constructs an answer from first principles.

We begin at the level of individual contracts, formulate the exact microscopic conservation law governing backlog, and derive by a functional law of large numbers and its central limit correction the continuum description analysed thereafter. The derivation determines, rather than assumes, the square-root form of the diffusion coefficients. We then take execution capacity as the key latent operational primitive and introduce a conversion law relating backlog and capacity to output, derived from the stationary work-in-system/throughput relation for a single-server queue. Output is therefore a derived quantity rather than a separately specified process, and the backlog roll-forward identity holds by construction. Capacity accumulates through a control representing hiring and mobilisation, chosen to maximise discounted margin net of convex adjustment cost and a schedule-overrun penalty.

The resulting state process is a three-dimensional degenerate diffusion on the closed positive orthant with deliberately non-affine drift. We establish, in a self-contained way, existence, pathwise uniqueness and invariance of the orthant; non-attainment of both degenerate faces under two explicit parameter inequalities; global Lipschitz dependence of the state flow on its initial condition in L1 and hence global Lipschitz continuity of the value function, although the same flow is only Hölder continuous of exponent one half in L2; existence of a viscosity solution of the associated Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation by vanishing viscosity using a closed-form global supersolution; complete Fichera classification of the boundary strata including the corner; closed-form real-analyticity of the linear reference resolvent at each degenerate face by reduction to Kummer's confluent hypergeometric equation; and a comparison principle based on an explicit logarithmic barrier. The comparison principle yields uniqueness of the viscosity solution in the class containing the value function and identifies it with the value function without requiring differentiability.

We also determine the Hessian of the conversion law in closed form. Its determinant equals the negative square of the minimum contract scale divided by the fourth power of the congestion denominator; joint concavity therefore occurs exactly when that scale vanishes, which is excluded by the corner regularity requirement. A linear-quadratic reduction about the interior steady state shows that the open-loop spectrum is real and stable, that the exogenous mode is uncontrollable but harmless, and that oscillation is a closed-loop phenomenon compatible with optimality whereas divergence is not. We further establish three-times-continuous differentiability of the value function across the free boundary associated with the hiring floor, with an explicit jump in the fourth derivative. One higher-regularity section is conditional on an external weighted Schauder/Kimura theory hypothesis and is explicitly separated from the unconditional results.

Finally, we confront the construction with nineteen years of disclosures from one large contractor. Both floor conditions hold by roughly two orders of magnitude. The disclosed backlog-to-output ratio decomposes, through an exact identity, into congestion and execution-duration components in a ratio of roughly three to one, so that interpreting the ratio as mean project duration overstates that duration by about fourfold. A falsifiable prediction is also tested: because congestion and high utilisation coincide within the model, a rising ratio accompanied by falling sector capacity utilisation cannot be generated by congestion at constant parameters; the data instead indicate a lengthening execution technology rather than a capacity shortfall. Tests of the congestion specification within the firm over time and across a small peer cross-section give differing results, separating a scale effect from a time trend; joint concavity is not established empirically.

title: Algorithmic Risk Profiling under GST: Transparency, Natural Justice and Taxpayer Rights in India Zeba
affiliations: Jamia hamdard, Hamdard Institute of Legal Studies and Research

detail.title: Algorithmic Risk Profiling under GST: Transparency, Natural Justice and Taxpayer Rights in India Zeba

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests, personal relationships, or affiliations that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is based on doctrinal legal research and analysis of statutes, judicial decisions, government documents, and academic literature. It does not involve human participants, personal data, interviews, surveys, or clinical investigations. Therefore, ethics committee approval was not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant, funding, or financial support from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: The increasing digitalisation of tax administration has transformed the operation of the Goods and Services Tax (GST) regime in India. Through the Goods and Services Tax Network (GSTN), tax authorities increasingly rely on data analytics, automated compliance tools, and risk-based assessment mechanisms to identify potentially non-compliant taxpayers. One of the most significant developments in this area is the use of algorithmic risk profiling, whereby taxpayers may be classified as high-risk based on data-driven indicators derived from GST returns, einvoices, e-way bills, and other digital records. While such systems may enhance administrative efficiency, improve compliance monitoring, and assist in detecting tax evasion, they also raise important legal and constitutional concerns. This article examines the implications of algorithmic risk profiling within the Indian GST framework, focusing on issues of transparency, accountability, and procedural fairness. It analyses the challenges posed by opaque or "black-box" decision-making systems, particularly where taxpayers are subjected to scrutiny, audits, refund restrictions, or other adverse actions without being informed of the reasons underlying their risk classification. The article evaluates these concerns through the lens of the principles of natural justice, the requirement of reasoned decision-making, and the constitutional guarantee against arbitrary state action under Article 14 of the Constitution of India. It further explores the emerging concept of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) as a mechanism for enhancing transparency and protecting taxpayer rights in automated administrative processes. Drawing upon comparative developments in jurisdictions such as the European Union, the United Kingdom, and Australia, the article argues that technological innovation in tax administration must be accompanied by appropriate safeguards to ensure fairness, accountability, and effective legal remedies. It concludes that a transparent and human-supervised approach to algorithmic governance is essential for maintaining public trust and protecting taxpayer rights in India's evolving digital tax ecosystem.

title: The Projected-Bias Policy for Dual Sourcing Problems
affiliations: Tsinghua University - Department of Industrial Engineering, Soochow University and University of British Columbia (UBC) - Sauder School of Business

detail.title: The Projected-Bias Policy for Dual Sourcing Problems

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We use AI to polish the work and assist with the numerical experiments.
declarations.funderStatement: Some authors are funded by the Chinese NSF.

detail.abstract: In the classic dual-sourcing inventory problem, a firm combines a low-cost regular source with a faster but more expensive express source. Constant regular orders simplify this allocation but cannot respond to changes in inventory and scheduled deliveries. We study how to make regular ordering responsive to this information while improving on established sourcing policies. Methodology/results: We propose the projected-bias (PB) policy, which combines inventory projection with a one-dimensional measure of future costs under a tailored base-surge (TBS) policy. For every admissible TBS parameter pair, PB has no higher long-run average cost than its TBS benchmark for every lead time. We also construct simpler policies that retain this guarantee through bias screening: they accept a proposed order when its projected-bias score is no greater than the TBS order's score, and otherwise use TBS. With immediate express supply and an exponential demand tail, we characterize the TBS parameter conditions under which PB coincides with the projected expedited-inventory-position (PE) policy, allowing implementation without bias evaluation. Screening PB orders against a capped dual-index (CDI) policy yields a CDI-screened PB policy (CSPB) with no higher average cost than its CDI benchmark. Across 216 instances, optimized PE and CDI have average optimality gaps of 0.52% and 0.64%. PB and CSPB nevertheless close, on average, 53.23% and 70.69% of PE's remaining optimality gap, and 57.01% and 73.57% of CDI's, respectively. Managerial implications: Responsive regular ordering can reduce sourcing and backlog costs, but the inventory needed to achieve these gains matters. PB improves TBS; CSPB can improve PB further by screening PB proposals with CDI continuation costs. Against strong PE and CDI alternatives, total-cost improvements can capture much of the remaining opportunity. Screening protects its chosen benchmark, while its value relative to the proposed policy depends on the resulting inventory balance.

title: The Small-Files Problem in Databricks Delta Lake: A Documentation-Grounded Analysis of OPTIMIZE, VACUUM, and Their Cost Implications
affiliations: Meghnad Saha Institute of Technology

detail.title: The Small-Files Problem in Databricks Delta Lake: A Documentation-Grounded Analysis of OPTIMIZE, VACUUM, and Their Cost Implications

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Declaration of Interest Statement Manuscript title: "The Small-Files Problem in Databricks Delta Lake: A Documentation-Grounded Analysis of OPTIMIZE, VACUUM, and Their Cost Implications" Author: FNU Aditya Ranjan The author declares that he has no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper. Signature: FNU Aditya Ranjan FNU Aditya Ranjan Date: 13-Sept-2026
declarations.funderStatement: No external fund used.

detail.abstract: This paper is primarily a documentation-grounded technical analysis rather than a Databricks benchmark study; most figures either restate official Databricks and AWS documentation directly or are arithmetic computed from officially published unit prices, clearly labeled as such throughout, with one explicit exception: a genuinely executed, independently reproduced local filesystem experiment (Section V), scoped explicitly as a general I/O proxy rather than a Databricks-specific measurement. The small-files problem-the accumulation of many small Parquet files under a Delta Lake table, degrading query performance independent of total data volume-is a welldocumented consequence of Delta Lake's append-only, ACIDtransactional write model, compounded by frequent small writes from streaming micro-batches or row-level MERGE, UPDATE, and DELETE operations. We document Databricks' four primary remediation mechanisms as officially specified: the OPTIMIZE command's bin-packing compaction, which is idempotent and preserves snapshot-isolated reads; Auto Compaction, unconditionally enabled for MERGE, UPDATE, and DELETE operations since Databricks Runtime 10.4 LTS; VACUUM, which removes files no longer referenced by table history after a retention window governed by the delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration property, defaulting to seven days; and Predictive Optimization, which automatically schedules OPTIMIZE, VACUUM, and ANALYZE on Unity Catalog managed tables and has been enabled by default for accounts created on or after November 11, 2024. We separately construct an illustrative, precisely computed cost model using Amazon S3's own published request pricing ($0.005 per 1,000 PUT/LIST requests, $0.0004 per 1,000 GET requests), showing that for a fixed 100 GB table scanned 1,000 times daily, fragmenting the same data volume from 100 files into 1,000,000 files increases modeled monthly S3 request cost from $1.35 to $12,150.00-a computed illustration of the mechanism, not a measured result. Separately, a genuinely executed local filesystem experiment, fixing a 200 MB total data volume and varying file count from 20 to 200,000, measured a 2,053-fold increase in directory-listing time and a 56fold increase in full-read time, real evidence that file-count-driven I/O overhead is a measurable phenomenon, explicitly scoped as a general proxy rather than a Delta Lake or S3 measurement. We synthesize all of this into a configuration reference and a practitioner decision framework, and state explicitly, in a dedicated limitations section, that every quantitative claim in this paper should be independently validated against a reader's own workload before being relied upon operationally.

title: Repression by Collective Responsibility
affiliations: Stanford Graduate School of Business

detail.title: Repression by Collective Responsibility

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant.

detail.abstract: Why knowingly punish people for the actions of others? I model a ruler designing a responsibility relation (a directed network specifying who is punished for whose behavior) to maximize obedience. There is a trade-off between "horizontal" and "vertical" deterrence: holding someone responsible for others gives her reason to police them; if she polices them, they obey more, but she risks punishment even when she obeys, so she obeys less. Individual responsibility is therefore uniquely optimal when policing is prohibitively costly or peer sanctions sufficiently weak, but never optimal when policing is cheap and peer sanctions strong. Obedience incentives can propagate through the network, so few responsibility links can generate dense policing. If people also suffer from others' punishment, the ruler can exploit their altruistic ties through responsibility, creating additional incentives to obey and police. With collective responsibility, rulers organize repression through relationships among the governed.

title: No Limited Liability for AI
affiliations: Columbia University - Law School, Yale University - Law School and Columbia University

detail.title: No Limited Liability for AI

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We are beneficial owners of public companies involved in AI through the index funds in our retirement accounts.
declarations.funderStatement: There research received no specific funding beyond the general research support offered by our institutions.

detail.abstract: Frontier AI labs should not have limited liability for torts. When a company commits a tort it cannot pay for, limited liability caps shareholders' losses at the value of their shares and lets the rest fall on the public. In effect, this makes limited liability a subsidy for risks borne by others. Scholars have long argued the subsidy distorts firm incentives. We argue the distortion is uniquely severe for firms that train frontier AI models. Its size depends on the covariance between private return and social harm, and on the shape of the tail of harmful outcomes. On both counts frontier AI is an extreme case. By the industry's own account, profit and risk strongly correlate, and the tail is fat and unbounded. A liability rule also has an informational advantage over substantive regulation because it does not require the state to understand the technology. We propose that all shareholders of frontier AI companies bear capped liability for torts in proportion to their holdings, with controlling shareholders weighted more heavily. We answer the principal objections, including the race with China, and note that state law permits firms to adopt this rule on their own.

title: Out with the new, in with the old? Supranational bank supervision and the composition of firm investment
affiliations: European Central Bank (ECB) - Directorate General Research, European Central Bank (ECB) and Florence School of Banking and Finance

detail.title: Out with the new, in with the old? Supranational bank supervision and the composition of firm investment
detail.abstract: Using exogenous variation generated by the creation of the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM) in the euro area, we find that relative to firms borrowing from banks subject to national supervision, firms borrowing from banks subject to supranational supervision reduce their share of intangible assets. This effect does not pre-date the supervisory reform and it does not obtain in non-SSM jurisdictions. The reallocation of investment away from intangible assets is stronger for small and young firms and appears to be driven by a short-term reduction in lending and a persistent increase in collateral standards.

title: The Wrong-pockets Birthday: Unfunded Permission, Coercive Extension, and the Missing Funding Stream at the End of Juvenile Supervision
affiliations: Penitents Grace, Inc

detail.title: The Wrong-pockets Birthday: Unfunded Permission, Coercive Extension, and the Missing Funding Stream at the End of Juvenile Supervision

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder and executive director of Credible Messengers United (Penitents Grace, Inc.), a Houston organization providing peer mentoring and workforce services to justice-involved young people. Organizations like it could receive funds under the design this paper proposes, and the author has advocated publicly for policy changes addressing this gap. Section 9 of the paper states how this interest shaped its scope.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The paper analyzes public statutes, regulations, agency documents, and legislative records and involves no human participants.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific funding from any agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Texas law already permits the support that young people leaving juvenile probation most often lack. Since 2017, Texas Human Resources Code § 142.007 has allowed a juvenile probation department to offer voluntary mentoring, job training, education, substance use, and behavioral health services for up to six months after discharge, whatever the young person's age. The permission carries no appropriation. It depends on "existing resources," and those resources are allocated, spent, and evaluated around youth who are still under supervision. This paper argues that the Texas arrangement is one instance of a general pattern. When spending authority, legal authority, and agency performance measures are organized around the same custodial boundary, a person who crosses that boundary loses most of the public support attached to them, and the loss reads as a budget shortfall rather than a design choice. The paper reads the legislative record of the three states that have tried to extend original juvenile jurisdiction past age 18 (Connecticut, Massachusetts, and Vermont) against the voluntary post-exit designs located in Texas, Massachusetts, California, and federal child welfare law. The coercive route has proved politically fragile: enacted once, stalled at its second step, and rejected or unresolved elsewhere. Voluntary support after exit does exist, but only as unfunded permissions, discretionary agency programs, competitive grants, or eligibility borrowed from foster care. This search located no state with a dedicated, non-competitive funding stream attached to discharge from juvenile supervision itself. The paper specifies a two-channel funding design adapted from Michigan's Raise the Age Fund (2021 to 2025) and states three propositions. It reports no outcome data and does not show that the design would improve outcomes. Its central diagnosis would be wrong if Texas departments already spend substantially on post-discharge services from existing resources. Its political prediction would be wrong if voluntary designs draw the same objections that stalled jurisdiction extension.

title: Political Economy of Intergovernmental Transfers in Nepal: How Politics Shapes the Distribution of Grants and Special Funds
affiliations: Tribhuvan University

detail.title: Political Economy of Intergovernmental Transfers in Nepal: How Politics Shapes the Distribution of Grants and Special Funds

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This research was conducted independently and did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The analysis and conclusions presented are based solely on the interpretation of secondary data from the cited sources:
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently and did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
The 2015 Constitution established a complex fiscal-tiers framework to distribute resources among the three tiers of government in Nepal. This paper aims to assess the allocation of grants and special funds to local levels based on political considerations. The study uses secondary data from the National Natural Resources and Fiscal Commission, the Ministry of Finance, the Office of the Auditor General, the Supreme Court. Civil society. The research discovers that despite the constitutional rules and regulations, there are informal understandings among ruling party leaders about allocating grants and special funds to selected municipalities and provinces based on political considerations.

The National Natural Resources and Fiscal Commission Act 2017 recommend
providing equalization grants to the local governments through a transparent and scientific
mechanism. The equalization was supposed to be based on population (70%), area (15%),
Human Development Index (5%), and the level of underdevelopment areas (10%). However,
the special grant and complementary grants have been distributed according to political
considerations of the ruling party. For instance, the Constituency Development Fund has been
distributed to the provincial assemblies based on the constituency of the Member of
Parliament (MP). In the fiscal year 2026/27, the Sudurpashchim province got Rs 2.23 billion
from the constituency development fund, while Bagmati province received over Rs 4 billion
from the fund. Despite the Supreme Court ruling in 2023/24 that the unfettered allocation of
the constituency development fund was unconstitutional, the unconstitutional funding culture
persists in Nepal’s federalism.

The paper finds that the number of people living in a local administrative division is
negatively related to the amount of money allocated to it. For instance, the metropolitan cities
had fewer wards, wider areas, and higher population density than the other cities. However,
the metropolitan cities received 3.4% less per capita than other municipalities with the same
number of wards, area, and population. The study concludes that despite the constitutional
provisions, there are informal political considerations in allocating special funds and grants to
municipal and provincial levels.

title: Fertility Rebound in the Becker Quantity-Quality Model
affiliations: Ritsumeikan University

detail.title: Fertility Rebound in the Becker Quantity-Quality Model

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: JSPS (Grants-in-Aid for Scientific Research)

detail.abstract: Recent evidence from high-income countries documents a weakening, and possible reversal, of the negative income-fertility relationship. This paper revisits the canonical quantity-quality framework and characterizes the conditions for a fertility rebound. Income affects fertility through an income effect and a negative substitution effect from rising child-rearing costs. Their relative strength depends on preference curvature and children's initial human-capital endowment. These forces can make substitution dominate at lower income levels but weaken relative to the income effect as income rises. The analysis also explains why reversal does not arise under logarithmic utility and a standard human-capital specification.

title: Market Regimes and Model Uncertainty in Portfolio Construction: Select or Diversify?
affiliations: Bank of Spain

detail.title: Market Regimes and Model Uncertainty in Portfolio Construction: Select or Diversify?

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author reports no potential conflict of interest. The opinions and analyses presented are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect those of Banco de España or the Eurosystem.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Building a portfolio requires choosing a construction method (minimum-variance, maximum-Sharpe, risk parity, or a hierarchical method) whose relative performance shifts over time, exposing the investor to model uncertainty beyond the parameter uncertainty these methods are designed to address. We ask whether the observable market state carries information about which method will perform better next period, beyond the methods' own recent performance. Framing the test as one of conditional predictive ability, we find that it does: a state defined by realized volatility predicts relative method performance, with the effect concentrated in the most estimation-dependent method, consistent with an estimation-stress channel. The signal survives permutation, wrong-mapping, and strong-benchmark placebos. Exploiting it yields economic value net of costs: a state-conditional selector significantly outperforms performance-chasing, while its advantage over diversification is positive but not significant. The case for selection over performance-chasing tends to be stronger when methods disagree more. Model uncertainty at the construction stage is, in part, predictable from the market state.

title: Data as an Input of Market Power: Competition, Privacy and Regulation of Digital Platforms in Kenya and South Africa
affiliations: University of Nairobi, School of Law

detail.title: Data as an Input of Market Power: Competition, Privacy and Regulation of Digital Platforms in Kenya and South Africa

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: This paper seeks to examine how competition law in Kenya and South Africa is adapting to treat data, rather than price, as the principal input through which digital platforms acquire and entrench market power. It argues that South Africa has moved furthest, writing data-related factors into its 2018 Competition Amendment Act and testing them through the GovChat v Facebook dominance dispute and two major platform market inquiries, while Kenya is only now legislating the same recognition through its pending Competition (Amendment) Bill. The paper contends that both jurisdictions, despite this doctrinal progress, have failed to bridge competition regulation with their separate data protection regimes, leaving privacy harms and competitive harms analysed in institutional isolation from one another. Drawing on comparative doctrine, the two countries' market inquiries and pending legislation, and international theoretical work on data-driven dominance, the paper builds toward an inter-regulator framework treating data access as a structural barrier to entry rather than a mere qualitative factor. It closes with jurisdictionspecific recommendations for Kenya and South Africa aimed at closing the coordination gap between competition and privacy regulation before digital platform power becomes further entrenched.

title: Foreign Direct Investment In Nigeria: The Legal Protection Of Investors Under Nigerian Law
affiliations: Nigerian Law School, Lagos

detail.title: Foreign Direct Investment In Nigeria: The Legal Protection Of Investors Under Nigerian Law

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships with any person or organization that could be perceived to have influenced this study.

declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Nigeria's legal architecture for foreign direct investment, anchored by the Nigerian Investment Promotion Commission Act 1995, the Foreign Exchange (Monitoring and Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1995, the Companies and Allied Matters Act 2020, constitutional property protections, and over thirty bilateral investment treaties, is on paper substantively robust and internationally competitive. This essay argues that the persistent gap between Nigeria's statutory promise and investor experience lies not in the design of these protections but in their implementation. Using the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission's 2024 blockage of Shell's 2.4 billion dollar onshore divestment as a case study, the essay examines the core substantive protections available to foreign investors, expropriation safeguards, fair and equitable treatment, free repatriation of capital, and access to investor state arbitration under ICSID and UNCITRAL rules, against the practical obstacles that undermine them: bureaucratic inertia, institutional overlap, corruption, foreign exchange policy volatility, and weak domestic enforcement of arbitral awards. It concludes with a set of institutional reforms, including a unified digital investment portal, embedded anti-corruption safeguards, a cross-party National Investment Stability Charter, and specialised commercial court divisions, aimed at converting Nigeria's legal promise into investor reality. Written as an entry for the Moroom Africa Essay Contest 2026.

title: Global Warming, Corporate Climate Sensitivities, and Stock Returns: US State-Level Evidence
affiliations: VinUniversity

detail.title: Global Warming, Corporate Climate Sensitivities, and Stock Returns: US State-Level Evidence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest to be declared. As the principle and only investigator, the corresponding sole author has all the rights reserved for the research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: As the principle and only investigator, the corresponding sole author has all the rights reserved for the research.

detail.abstract: There are growing debates on the pricing of climate risks with (dis)appearing premiums demanded by investors. Employing extensive local climate data, the current study examines the market pricings of corporate climate sensitivity (CCS) with stock return predictability. Using our forecasted market-based CCS measure, the study shows that investors demand premiums when corporate stocks are exposed to global warming phenomena across the US states. Climate premium demands significantly appear when corporate stocks are prone to local disaster risk, while they remain marginally statistically significant for local transition risk. We do not observe the appearance of carbon premium for both direct and interacting effects on stock return predictions. The findings highlight the robust pricing of the systematic risks of global warming with the climate premium demanded by investors. We recognize detectable premium demands for various climate risks, while our market-based CCS measures present their dominant robustness across the risk drivers over the past decades. The study complements prior literature on the (mis)pricing of climate and carbon risks, shedding light on potential research directions for future studies.

title: Shaping Climate-Tech Private Capital: The Role of the Paris Agreement in Fundraising
affiliations: Fairleigh Dickinson University, ESC Clermont Business School, University Jean Moulin Lyon 3 and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: This study examines whether the Paris Agreement (PA) affects private capital fundraising in technologies that support decarbonization, hereafter "climate-tech." Using data on private capital funds created between November 2010 and October 2022, we find that the PA nearly doubles climate-tech fund creation relative to non-climate-tech funds, which is a statistically and economically significant effect. Post-PA climate-tech funds are created predominantly by new entrants-managing firms that enter climate-tech only after the PA and account for 70.4% of all such funds. However, we find no statistically significant post-PA increase in the size of climate-tech funds relative to non-climate-tech funds. These results suggest that the PA affects climate-tech fundraising primarily through the creation of more funds rather than through larger capital commitments per fund. Our evidence indicates that the PA shapes the supply of private capital available for decarbonization investment.

title: The Impact of Natural Disasters on Syndicated Lending: Evidence from Europe
affiliations: University of Amsterdam - Faculty of Economics & Econometrics (FEE) and University of Amsterdam

detail.title: The Impact of Natural Disasters on Syndicated Lending: Evidence from Europe
detail.abstract: This paper examines how syndicated loan originations respond to natural disasters across European regions between 2000 and 2024. We combine geographically identified disaster events from the EM-DAT database with syndicated loan data from DealScan and estimate the dynamic response of lending using panel local projections. To account for differences in the economic consequences of disasters across regions, we measure regional economic exposure using population density. We find that syndicated loan originations decline significantly following natural disasters, with the largest contraction occurring approximately two months after the event. The results are robust across alternative country samples, estimation periods, and measures of disaster severity based on reported economic damages. We also document considerable heterogeneity across disaster types, with floods and storms accounting for most of the decline. Our findings suggest that natural disasters temporarily disrupt large-scale corporate financing, highlighting syndicated lending as an important transmission channel for climate-related shocks.

title: Are Guidelines Worth Following? Decision-Making Under Incomplete Evidence
affiliations: Yale School of Management, Harvard University and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Are Guidelines Worth Following? Decision-Making Under Incomplete Evidence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.
declarations.funderStatement: None.

detail.abstract:
Medical guidelines translate clinical evidence into treatment rules, but the evidence may identify treatment benefits more clearly than harms. We study anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation, combining randomized trials with Veterans Health Administration data. Trial evidence reveals substantial heterogeneity in stroke-prevention benefits but does not reliably identify how treatment-induced bleeding harms vary across patients. In the target population, patients with larger predicted stroke benefits also have higher untreated bleeding risk, making this ambiguity consequential. We evaluate existing guidelines and develop maximin and minimax-regret treatment rules robust to alternative harm structures. At a benchmark preventing 50% of preventable strokes, robust rules induce 33-41% fewer bleeds than random treatment and outperform existing guidelines. Finite-sample uncertainty generates noticeable instability in fine patient rankings but little instability in treatment assignments or welfare. Physician performance and the relationship between guideline adherence and skill also depend substantially on assumptions about how treatment-induced bleeding harms vary across patients.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

title: What Survives an FOMC Surprise? Confounding and the Persistence of Announcement Effects in Asset Prices
affiliations: New York University

detail.title: What Survives an FOMC Surprise? Confounding and the Persistence of Announcement Effects in Asset Prices

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: Every FOMC announcement moves asset prices twice: once for the surprise in it, once for everything else. How much confounding would it take to overturn the first, and does either last? In 261 scheduled announcements, 1994-2026, no impact response of stocks, yields, exchange rates or foreign equities is overturned by a confounder as strong as the news that predicts surprises. What follows does not last: monetary momentum unwinds within a month, the post-FOMC yield drift disappears with the full surprise factor, and the Fed information effect reverses the next day. The surprise persists; the rest reverts.

title: The Relationship between Perceived Gender-based Labor Market Exclusion and Post-entrepreneurial Precarity: Evidence from Women Entrepreneurs in Yemen
affiliations: University of Science and Technology (Yemen)

detail.title: The Relationship between Perceived Gender-based Labor Market Exclusion and Post-entrepreneurial Precarity: Evidence from Women Entrepreneurs in Yemen

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that no competing or conflicting interests affected the results of the study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Consent was obtained before participants could proceed with the questionnaire. Participation in the study's questionnaire was voluntary. No financial or non-financial incentives were offered to elicit participation. All participants' data collected were anonymized.

detail.abstract: This study examined the relationship between perceived gender-based employment discrimination and survivalist entrepreneurship conditions among women entrepreneurs in Yemen, thereby testing a central proposition of the Disadvantaged Labor Theory. Using a cross-sectional survey of 108 women entrepreneurs, the study measured employment discrimination through institutional failure, occupational segregation, and societal norms and assessed survivalist entrepreneurship through financial insecurity, venture fragility, and constrained economic mobility. Correlation tests and multiple regression analysis revealed a counterintuitive result: although respondents reported substantial employment discrimination and severe entrepreneurial precarity, employment discrimination did not significantly predict survivalist entrepreneurship. None of its three dimensions showed a significant relationship with survivalist conditions. Instead, household dependency and monthly business income explained meaningful variation in entrepreneurial precarity, while even a small income surplus distinguished less vulnerable ventures from businesses that barely covered basic needs. These findings challenge a simple linear account in which stronger labor market exclusion necessarily produces more survivalist ventures. They instead distinguish the structural forces that push women into entrepreneurship from the household and business conditions that shape venture outcomes after entry. By refining the Disadvantaged Labor Theory for a conflict-affected developing economy, the study demonstrates that policies supporting women's entrepreneurship in Yemen must combine labor market inclusion with working capital, income stabilization, household-sensitive assistance, and measures that strengthen venture resilience and economic mobility.

title: The Envy Cost of Strategy-proof and Ex-post Efficient Assignment
affiliations: Korea University - College of Political Science and Economics

detail.title: The Envy Cost of Strategy-proof and Ex-post Efficient Assignment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that they have no competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no funding.

detail.abstract: How much envy is unavoidable under strategy-proofness and ex-post efficiency? For every market size, we determine the minimum worstcase envy over all mechanisms satisfying these axioms on the full strictpreference domain. Envy is the largest positive cumulative-probability gap, equivalently the supremum of normalized expected-utility envy consistent with an agent's ranking. With n ≥ 3 agents and n distinct objects, the minimax value is ⌊(n-1) 2 /4⌋/[n(n-1)], attained by random serial dictatorship. The lower bound requires no anonymity or neutrality. Its proof combines incentive equalities, efficiency, and capacity balance on a four-report domain, without characterizing admissible mechanisms. The optimal loss converges to 1/4. With multiple copies of object types, exact envy-freeness is feasible under the same axioms precisely when the two smallest capacities sum to at least the number of agents.

title: A Tale of Two Days: Social Media Attention and Anomalies on News and Non-News Days

detail.abstract: Using StockTwits posts, more than 200 anomalies, and earnings and corporate news events, we show that social media attention suppresses anomaly returns on non-news days but amplifies them on news days. The news-day effect is consistent with attention facilitating the incorporation of information into prices. The non-news effect signifies increased anomaly mispricing, suggesting that high attention can amplify biased beliefs on such days. Significant contributions from both long- and short-leg stocks to these effects indicate that attention-driven buying price pressures play a minor role. Overall, social media attention appears to play a dual role for anomalies, decreasing mispricing on news days by facilitating information dissemination and increasing mispricing on non-news days by amplifying biased beliefs.

title: Social Exclusion, Institutional Support and the Perceived Criminal Involvement of Waste Pickers: Evidence from a Stakeholder Survey in Rawalpindi-Islamabad, Pakistan
affiliations: National Defence University

detail.title: Social Exclusion, Institutional Support and the Perceived Criminal Involvement of Waste Pickers: Evidence from a Stakeholder Survey in Rawalpindi-Islamabad, Pakistan

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: The study was conducted as part of the author's MPhil thesis at the National Defence University, Islamabad, under the supervisor's approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific funding.

detail.abstract:
Purpose. Informal waste pickers (locally kachray walay, or rag-pickers) are among the most marginalised urban groups in Pakistan, yet public debate often links them to petty crime, substance use and sex work. This study examines how frontline stakeholders-police personnel, NGO workers and other urban residents-perceive the criminal involvement of waste pickers in the twin cities of Rawalpindi and Islamabad, and whether those perceptions are associated with perceived social exclusion and perceived support from government and nongovernmental organisations (NGOs). 

Design. A cross-sectional survey was administered in 2020 to 300 stakeholders (police n = 78; NGO staff n = 175; other residents n = 47) recruited through convenience and snowball sampling. Three Likert-type scales measured perceived criminal involvement (PCI), social exclusion (SE) and perceived institutional support (PIS). Data were analysed with reliability tests, Pearson correlations and multiple regression; an indirect association of support with criminal involvement through exclusion was tested from the correlation matrix. 

Findings. Substance use (80%) and sex work (79%) were the offences most often attributed to waste pickers, whereas serious violent crime such as murder was rarely attributed (5%). Perceived social exclusion was strongly and positively associated with perceived criminal involvement (r = .73, p < .001). Perceived institutional support was weakly and negatively associated with criminal involvement (r =-.17, p = .004) and negatively associated with exclusion (r =-.30, p < .001). In the regression model (R² = .53), exclusion was the only significant predictor (β = .75, p < .001); the direct effect of support was not significant (β = .06, p = .148). The indirect association of support through reduced exclusion was significant (standardised indirect effect =-.23, Sobel z =-5.27, p < .001). 

Originality and implications. The results suggest that support programmes are associated with lower perceived criminality mainly insofar as they reduce exclusion. Cash transfers or anti-beggary removals that do not change waste pickers' social position are unlikely to change the risk profile stakeholders perceive. The paper argues for inclusion-oriented policy: 1 registration and integration of waste pickers into municipal solid-waste systems, protected access to social protection, and rights-based, non-extractive policing.

title: From Russian Dependence to Structural Realignment: European Energy Security Transition, 2010-2025
affiliations: Monash University - Monash University Malaysia

detail.title: From Russian Dependence to Structural Realignment: European Energy Security Transition, 2010-2025

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that he has no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or funding from any public, commercial, or not-for-profit organization. It was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper is the third in a three-paper series on energy export dependency and resilience, following studies of Qatar's LNG economy [16] and a four-country Gulf fiscal resilience comparison [17]. This paper turns from exporter-side dependency to importer-side adjustment, studying how five European Union countries, Germany, Poland, Italy, France, and Hungary, changed their gas import structure after Russia cut pipeline gas supply in 2022. Using a panel of 80 country-year observations from 2010 to 2025, the paper tests four propositions: that countries with higher pre-2022 Russian gas exposure faced a larger supply shock, adjusted at different speeds, paid different fiscal costs, and were protected to different degrees by structural assets built before the crisis. Russian gas exposure is measured using Eurostat's official trade statistics as the proportion of total gas imports sourced from Russia, and the results show Hungary, not Germany, held the highest proportional exposure in 2021. A Difference-inDifferences regression finds a positive relationship between exposure and post-2022 diversification, consistent with the paper's first proposition, though the estimate does not reach statistical significance at conventional levels, a limitation this paper attributes in part to the small number of countries in the panel. The remaining propositions are supported primarily through descriptive evidence on fiscal subsidy spending, LNG import volumes, and renewable energy shares. The paper argues that a country's proportional exposure, not its economic size or prominence in public commentary, better explains the pace and shape of its post-2022 energy realignment.

title: Remunerating means of Payment
affiliations: Frankfurt School of Finance and Management

detail.title: Remunerating means of Payment

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not applicable
declarations.ethicsApproval: This is not applicable to this kind of economic study.
declarations.funderStatement: This was written in the context of my non-resident fellowship with Bruegel, who contributed to the funding of the research (but I am also an independent researcher with a professor position)

detail.abstract: Though banknotes cannot technically earn interest, electronic means of payment can in principle be remunerated at negligible cost. Many countries however permit free remuneration only of bank sight deposits and reserves with the central bank. The European Union does not allow e-money, central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) or stablecoins to be remunerated. We review the literature and conclude that no economic theory of the interest-rate spread between money and adjacent financial assets implies that money must be unremunerated. Non-remuneration acts like a distortionary tax on money holders proportional to nominal interest rates and makes the inflation tax regressive, redistributing income from less-wealthy individuals to issuers. Moreover, such constraints are circumvented 'internally' through disguised remuneration or 'externally' through flight into neighbouring financial assets. The decline of transaction costs implied by universal electronification, open banking, agentic artificial intelligence and smart contracts, makes external circumvention all too easy, creating unintended flows of funds across the interest-rate cycle and thereby undermining financial stability. The main arguments for constraining remuneration-protecting the bank deposit franchise and financial stability-are insufficiently founded. They can be defended at most as temporary second-best measures when first-best instruments are unavailable. EU policymakers should therefore not defend non-remuneration as a matter of principle: the digital euro could rely on tiered remuneration, rather than on non-remuneration and holding limits, the EU ban on stablecoin remuneration should at minimum be restated as transitional, and the prohibition of emoney remuneration should be abolished in line with a pro-competition logic.

title: The Algebraic Geometry of Multi-Player Blotto Games
affiliations: Louisiana Tech University - Department of Economics and Finance

detail.title: The Algebraic Geometry of Multi-Player Blotto Games

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No competing interests.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding for this research.

detail.abstract: In a Blotto game, players divide budgets across battlefields. With two players, whether an equilibrium can be written in closed form depends on the contest technology and on whether battlefields aggregate (Canann, 2026). This paper studies any number of players. In lottery contests a weak player may sit out a battlefield, so each pattern of participation has its own equilibrium conditions. When all m players are active on all n battlefields, the conditions have exactly D(m-1, n-1) complex solutions for generic data, where D is a Delannoy number. The count is symmetric in players and battlefields, which reflects two potentials whose critical points are the solutions, one in relative prices and one in battlefield totals. The Galois group is the full symmetric group for all m, n ≥ 2, so beyond two players and two battlefields such an equilibrium generically has no formula in radicals. Equilibria in which a player sits out a battlefield solve smaller systems; with three players and two battlefields each such equilibrium that is an isolated solution of its equations has a formula in radicals. In all-pay contests, isolated equilibria in which the two strongest bidders on each battlefield are strictly ahead of the rest have degree bounded independently of the number of battlefields. With three players the class of such an equilibrium is read off the digraph of who outbids whom: it has a formula in radicals exactly when some player is never the weaker active bidder, and otherwise its degree is between 6 and 10 with the full symmetric group.

title: Dharmic Ethics and Behavioural Economics: Rethinking Sustainable Consumption through Ancient Indian Thought
affiliations: Global College (Malta), Global College (Malta)

detail.title: Dharmic Ethics and Behavioural Economics: Rethinking Sustainable Consumption through Ancient Indian Thought

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or funding from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or non-profit sectors. The study was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: Contemporary sustainability discourse is dominated by frameworks developed within the last half-century of Western environmental and economic thought. This paper argues that the textual corpus of Sanātana Dharma in particular the Bhagavad Gītā, the Īśā and Chāndogya Upaniṣads, the śānti Parva of the Mahābhārata, and cosmological material from the Purāṇas articulates, well over two millennia earlier, a coherent set of ethical propositions relevant to ecological restraint, resource stewardship, and collective welfare. The paper undertakes a qualitative, interpretive textual analysis of five constructs the yajña-cakra (cycle of reciprocity), aparigraha (non-accumulation), lokasaṃgraha (welfare of the world), pañca-mahābhūta (the five elements), and trusteeship and maps each onto the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). It then connects these constructs explicitly to specific theories in modern behavioural and institutional economics: choice architecture and nudge theory (Thaler & Sunstein), the default effect (Johnson & Goldstein; Pichert & Katsikopoulos), the consumption ratchet effect and relative-income hypothesis (Duesenberry), the incentive-design ratchet principle (Weitzman), and loss aversion and status-quo bias under prospect theory (Kahneman & Tversky) arguing that several textual constructs anticipate, on normative grounds, mechanisms this literature later validated empirically. The paper closes by acknowledging the interpretive and historiographical limitations of this approach and proposing directions for empirical follow-up research.

title: Yoga for Health Professionals

detail.abstract: This paper draws on the teachings and published research of Prof. Dr. Ananda Balayogi Bhavanani (Director, ISCM) and Prof. Madanmohan (Former Head Dept. of Physiology, Sri Balaji Vidyapeeth), makes the case that Yoga can restore the compassionate core of medical practice while offering measurable physiological benefit. It traces the yogic understanding of stress and disease, the kosha model of illness, and Yoga's mechanisms and modalities, then grounds these in evidence: a study showing 30-minute Shavasana reverses the autonomic effects of overnight sleep deprivation in young healthcare professionals, and a six-month trial showing improved well-being and reduced stress in healthcare students. Includes practical techniques for clinical settings.

title: Who Cooks When the Supermarket Cooks? The Value of Time and the Market Substitution of Domestic Food Preparation in Spain

detail.title: Who Cooks When the Supermarket Cooks? The Value of Time and the Market Substitution of Domestic Food Preparation in Spain

detail.abstract: Spanish households are buying more of their food with the cooking already done. We measure this with a Domestic Labour Substitution (DLS) index built on eleven food ladders-forms of the same food ordered by the preparation they displace from the home to the market-using the Spanish Ministry of Agriculture's household purchase panel for 2014-2025. A conditional-logit model of the choice among forms predicts that both a higher value of time and cheaper processed forms raise DLS, but that common price changes cancel in the gap between household groups shopping in the same market. Processed forms became relatively cheaper in 9 of 11 ladders, so prices explain part of the aggregate climb; regional growth in women's employment explains at most 28% of it. Among workingage households, those whose main shopper is economically active buy more preparation in 88% of ladder-years. During the 2020-2021 lockdown and restrictions, which kept active households at home, that gap fell to 27% of its earlier level (wild bootstrap p = 0.007) and partly reopened afterwards. Published household margins also reveal that most of the recent widening of the active-inactive gap is the growing weight of households over 65, who sit far lower on the ladder.

title: A Diversified, Multi-Stakeholder Funding Framework for the Long-Term Sustainability of India's Unified Payments Interface (UPI)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationship with any government body, financial institution, or payment application operator discussed in this paper that could be perceived to influence the study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This paper is a policy analysis based on publicly available government data and does not involve human participants, patient data, or primary data collection requiring ethics review.

detail.abstract: In September 2026, the Government of India reintroduced a Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) of 0.4 percent on Unified Payments Interface (UPI) person-to-merchant transactions exceeding ₹2,000, ending the zero-MDR regime that had been in place since 2020. This policy shift has generated significant public debate, with critics arguing that the government possesses sufficient alternative revenue, including record surpluses from the Reserve Bank of India (RBI), public sector bank dividends, and profits of the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), to fund UPI without levying a merchant fee. This paper examines the fiscal basis of that claim against the Union Government's official budget accounts for FY 2026-27, and finds that all cited non-tax revenue streams are already fully absorbed within a total receipts figure that falls ₹16.96 lakh crore short of total expenditure, a gap financed entirely through fresh borrowing. Building on this finding, the paper proposes an alternative to the current merchant-only MDR: a four-pillar diversified funding model comprising a fixed Union Budget allocation, a tiered (non-cliff) MDR structure, a cess on third-party payment application (TPAP) ancillary revenue, and a voluntary, low-cost annual "UPI Pass" for high-volume individual users. The paper details the design, revenue projections, classification safeguards against double taxation, comparative international precedent (Brazil's PIX system), and a mandated inflation-linked review mechanism intended to prevent the fee erosion observed historically in Indian ATM charges and capital gains taxation. The proposal is offered as a fiscally grounded, distributionally fairer alternative that avoids placing the entire cost burden on small and medium merchants.

title: The Labor Certification Process Was Not Built for AI Compliance Roles
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.abstract: The permanent labor certification process (PERM) tests job opportunities against Standard Occupational Classification codes and DOL wage levels calibrated to stable, codifiable occupations. This article examines the structural mismatch between that framework and AI-driven regulatory compliance for financial technology, a function that did not exist as a distinct occupational category when the current SOC taxonomy was last revised and that continues to be assembled across law, finance, and machine learning rather than staffed against a pre-existing job description. Drawing on 20 C.F.R. § 656.17(i)(1), a 2024 cluster of federal enforcement actions against sponsor banks documented elsewhere in this series, and survey data from the International Association of Privacy Professionals showing no settled organizational home for AI governance, the article argues that PERM's occupational and wage-level fixity is poorly suited to test the value of this work. It concludes by situating that mismatch within the third prong of Matter of Dhanasar, arguing that the classification gap is a documented, data-supported feature of the field's immaturity rather than an assumption.

detail.abstract: Private credit funds often report different values for the same loan. We study whether valuation incentives explain these disagreements. Paying investors at NAV appears to constrain reported valuations.

detail.abstract: Public debt-collection announcements are an observation process, not a record of economic outcomes. This note asks a narrow, fully specified question about that process. After a debtor name that has already appeared in a newspaper's debt-collection announcements passes an activity-screened 12-month non-observation windowtwelve consecutive months in which no publication of that name is observed and in which every calendar month passes a pre-frozen publication-activity screen-in what share of cases is the name actually observed to be published again within 6, 12, 18 and 24 months? Using the Jiangnan Times announcement column and a frozen first-silence landmark design whose eligibility test uses no information dated after the landmark, we report 1 of 428 (0.23%), 9 of 428 (2.1%), 11 of 428 (2.57%) and 19 of 428 (4.44%) observed re-publications. The cohort of 428 canonical debtor identities is the identity-corrected, row-traceable result of an adjudicated identity review: of 6,014 canonical Jiangnan Times debtor names, 1,501 never complete an activity-screened 12-month nonobservation window before the freeze, and 4,085 fail the pre-frozen activity screen over [silence start, landmark]. The screen records that the channel was demonstrably publishing, not that its archive is complete; the term nonobservation is used for that reason. Because the numerator counts only observed re-publications, every figure is a lower bound: a debtor recorded as NOT_OBSERVED is not an exit, not a non-event and not evidence of economic survival. The one substantive concentration we cannot remove is disclosed rather than smoothed: a single announcement batch supplies 44.63% of the cohort and 9 of the 19 twenty-four-month observed republications. Removing the most adverse single origin batch lowers the twenty-four-month lower bound to 3.31%; removing the most adverse single future-event batch lowers it to 3.271%. Taken together, the most conservative single-batch statement of either kind is 3.27%.

detail.abstract:
Objective. To evaluate the extent to which the world's largest and most well established Conditional Cash Transfer (CCT) program, the Bolsa Família Program (BFP), reduced health inequities in the incidence of AIDS, tuberculosis (TB), and child mortality in Brazil. Design. Health impact evaluation within a large-scale cohort study.
Setting. Brazil, from January 1 2004 to December 31 2015. Participants. We use three cohorts totaling 92,382,204 million individuals: i) Cohort 1: 22,788,997 individuals aged 13 and older from 2007 to 2015 for the analysis of AIDS incidence; ii) Cohort 2: 54,759,252 individuals from 2004 to 2015 for the analysis of TB incidence; iii) Cohort 3: 14,833,955 children under the age of 5 from 2004 to 2015 for the analysis of child mortality.
Interventions. We began by assessing the excess incidence and mortality attributable to poverty severity. To estimate the reduction in health inequities associated with the BFP, we applied multiple inequality indices. We then conducted impact evaluations of BFP’s effects across wealth deciles, employing Inverse Probability Treatment Weighting (IPTW) multivariable Poisson regressions adjusted for all relevant socioeconomic, demographic, and health variables at the individual, household, and municipal levels. 
Main outcome measures. Incidence of AIDS, incidence of TB, and child mortality Results. Receiving BFP benefits eliminated the excess incidence and mortality associated with extreme poverty, significantly reducing the Gini, Theil, and Concentration Index values. Among the extremely poor, BFP was associated with reductions in the incidence of AIDS by 49%(RR: 0.51;95%CI:0.48-0.54), TB by 51%(RR:0.49;95%CI:0.48-0.50), and child mortality by 70%(RR:0.30;95%CI:0.28 0.32). These effects diminished progressively as beneficiaries’ poverty levels decreased. Over the past two decades, BFP is estimated to have prevented 99,083 cases of AIDS, 235,489 of TB, and 200,627 child deaths. 
Conclusions. Conditional Cash Transfer programs can significantly alleviate the burden of AIDS, tuberculosis, and child mortality, with the most pronounced impacts observed among the poorest populations. Their effectiveness follows a gradient aligned with levels of individual vulnerability and can substantially reduce health inequities in low- and middle-income countries.

title: Economic Mechanisms for Implementation of Hydrogen Projects under Global Energy Transition

detail.title: Economic Mechanisms for Implementation of Hydrogen Projects under Global Energy Transition
detail.abstract: The global hydrogen industry is expanding, driven by climate commitments, heightened energy insecurity and innovation trends that are transforming the global economic and energy landscape. This paper examines business practice in the implementation of hydrogen projects in the context of the global energy transition, focusing on the national hydrogen strategies of market leaders. The study aims at identifying the most promising economic and financial mechanisms for hydrogen energy development which can be scaled up in the future. The paper compares hydrogen production methods by carbon footprint, efficiency and cost, classifies the hydrogen strategies of the selected countries into import-oriented, export-oriented and self-sufficiency models, and determines their hydrogen industry development models with regard to resource endowment and climate goals. The paper finds that the existing economic and financial mechanisms for stimulating hydrogen demand are effective provided that corporate demand for hydrogen is robust. The study concludes that further research into global practice of hydrogen project implementation is needed as hydrogen energy scales up worldwide.

detail.abstract: Enterprise artificial intelligence is often seen in the context of the capability of the models used, data availability, technology infrastructure, or responsible AI governance. But organizations might have all these things but still face challenges in scaling their AI in the business processes. The argument presented in this paper is that the problem is both organizational and technical. The success of enterprise AI requires a coherent set of capabilities covering data quality, data governance, data products, data contracts, AI platform, accountability, lineage, explainability, ownership, value measurement, and operating model. The main proposition developed in this paper is that capability coherence is essential for scaling enterprise AI. The paper explores the proposition via conceptual synthesis of 12 practitioner essays published between July and September 2026 on the topics including data quality and governance, data products, AI ecosystems, responsible AI, decision traceability, data ownership, governance value, and AI-native operating models. The practitioner corpus is considered together with existing research and institutional literature, including BCBS 239, NIST AI Risk Management Framework, data-mesh research, IT governance, and dynamic capabilities theory.

title: Why Is Manufacturing Productivity Growth So Low?

detail.title: Why Is Manufacturing Productivity Growth So Low?
detail.abstract:
We examine the recent slow growth in manufacturing productivity. We show that nearly all measured TFP growth since 1987—and its post-2000s decline—comes from a few computer-related industries. We argue conventional measures understate manufacturing productivity growth by failing to fully capture quality improvements. We compare consumer to producer and import price indices. In rapidly changing industries, consumer price indices indicate less inflation, suggesting mismeasurement in standard industry deflators. Using an input-output framework, we estimate that TFP growth is understated by 1.7 percentage points in durable manufacturing and 0.4 percentage points in nondurable manufacturing, with no mismeasurement in nonmanufacturing industries.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

detail.abstract: Calls for global regulation of frontier artificial intelligence have multiplied, but they rarely specify what such regulation would have to contain, who would exercise which powers, and how the arrangement would survive rivalry between the states that matter most. This paper introduces the Global Frontier AI Safety Framework, a reference architecture that attempts that specification, and the regulatory stack that develops it, deposited separately on Zenodo. The Framework pairs a model domestic statute with a framework convention. Domestic regulators license, supervise, pause and contain; an international technical body sets evaluation criteria and, for the highest-risk systems, must concur before release. Authority is asymmetric: any responsible body may restrict on its own, but none may approve alone. Testing runs in sealed environments on the developer's own hardware, so that no state has to surrender its models. This introductory briefing maps the field as of September 2026: United Nations scientific and dialogue bodies, the Council of Europe convention, European Union obligations for generalpurpose models, national evaluation institutes, parallel initiatives led by China and the United States, industry frameworks, and academic model treaties. It finds more institution-building than is often assumed, but little binding control over frontier development. It then sets out where the Framework follows emerging convergence, what it borrows, and what it adds. The main valueadded contributions are a worked interface that turns protected evaluation evidence into domestic permission, decision rules designed for rivalry, and systematic stress-testing of legal feasibility, failure modes and regime-induced concentration. The Framework is a design standard, not a forecast; its usefulness does not depend on adoption. This briefing closes with lessons that may carry over to other proposals, and a guide to the stack.
